title: The Missing Corners
problem: Remove two diagonally opposite corner squares from a standard 8-by-8 checkerboard. Can the remaining 62 squares be tiled exactly with 31 dominoes, each covering two edge-adjacent squares? Prove your answer.

hints.text: Track a property that every domino preserves.
Every edge-adjacent domino covers one black square and one white square.

solution.setup: Use the standard alternating black-and-white coloring of the board.
solution.reasoning: Opposite corners of an even-by-even checkerboard have the same color. Removing them leaves 30 squares of that color and 32 of the other. Every domino placed on edge-adjacent squares covers exactly one black and one white square, so any domino tiling would cover equal numbers of both colors. The remaining board does not have equal color counts.
solution.finalAnswer: No; such a tiling is impossible.
solution.sanityCheck: Thirty-one dominoes cover 31 squares of each color, but the mutilated board has color counts 30 and 32.

keyInsight: A coloring invariant can prove impossibility without attempting to enumerate tilings.
recognitionCues: A local move always affects colored classes in a fixed way, while the target configuration has incompatible class counts.
commonMistakes: Arguing only that 62 is even; area is necessary but not sufficient for tileability.
followUps: Does the answer change if one black corner and one white corner are removed? Is equal color count sufficient?

source.notes: Original exposition of the classic mutilated-checkerboard invariant.

verification.notes: Every domino covers one square of each color, but the remainder has a 30-to-32 split.
